title: Sizing a help-centre bot
scenario: Your team is planning a help-centre assistant. Each request will include a system prompt, two tool definitions, the user's question and up to three help articles. A teammate built the first estimate from word counts in a spreadsheet (exhibit). Nothing is live yet. You must decide how to turn this sketch into numbers you can trust.
exhibit:
Estimate v1 (from word counts, 0.75 words per token)

system prompt        600 words   ->   800 tokens
user question         30 words   ->    40 tokens
3 help articles     2,700 words  -> 3,600 tokens
------------------------------------------------
input per request                   4,440 tokens

Notes:
- measured on model A last quarter
- launch plan says: use model B (newer)
- 20% of articles are in Japanese

questions.prompt: What is the biggest gap in Estimate v1 as an input-token count?

options.text: It leaves out the two tool definitions, which are also input tokens.
options.explanation: Right. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are sent as input. In the Claude token counting docs, a one-sentence question with one small tool defined counts 403 input tokens.

options.text: It counts the system prompt, but the system prompt is free and never billed.
options.explanation: The system prompt is part of the request and counts as input. The token counting endpoint includes system prompts in its total.

options.text: It should count output tokens in the input total.
options.explanation: Output tokens are counted and priced separately from input. Mixing them hides the real cost shape.

options.text: It is complete. Word counts are exact for every model.
options.explanation: Word-to-token ratios are a rough rule for English. They are not exact, and the estimate already misses the tools.

questions.prompt: The counts were measured on model A, but launch uses model B, a newer model. What should the team do?

options.text: Recount every prompt with model B, because a different tokenizer can give a different count for the same text.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say newer models use a newer tokenizer (about 30% more tokens for the same text) and advise recounting against the model you plan to use.

options.text: Reuse model A's counts. The text has not changed, so the tokens have not changed and the launch budget stands.
options.explanation: Same text does not mean same tokens. The count depends on the model's tokenizer.

options.text: Keep model A's counts but add a 10% safety margin. That covers any tokenizer change between the two models.
options.explanation: A guessed margin is not a measurement. The documented change was larger than that. Recount on model B.

options.text: Skip counting and wait for the first invoice.
options.explanation: You can measure before launch. Counting tools and test calls give real numbers before real users pay the cost.

questions.prompt: 20% of the articles are in Japanese. How should that change the estimate?

options.text: Measure real Japanese articles with a counting tool. The 0.75-words rule is for English only.
options.explanation: Right. Both vendors give the 4-characters / 0.75-words rule for English text, and Anthropic's FAQ says the count varies by language and content type. Measure instead of guessing.

options.text: No change. Tokens are the same in every language.
options.explanation: The rule of thumb is stated for English. Other languages can split differently, so the rule may be wrong for them.

options.text: Count the Japanese articles at half the English rate. Shorter scripts use fewer tokens, so the total drops.
options.explanation: There is no such rule. Non-English text often uses more tokens, not fewer. Measure a sample.

options.text: Count Japanese words with the same spreadsheet formula.
options.explanation: Using the English ratio for another language is the exact mistake to avoid. Measure a sample instead.

questions.prompt: After launch, which number should the cost dashboard use as the source of truth?

options.text: The usage block of each response (input and output tokens actually used).
options.explanation: Right. Each response reports the tokens it used. A pre-call count is an estimate; the Claude docs say it can differ by a small amount.

options.text: The pre-call token counting result, because it is exact down to the last token.
options.explanation: The Claude docs call the token count an estimate. It is good for planning, not for billing truth.

options.text: The word count of each message times 0.75.
options.explanation: That is a rough rule for English. It is the least accurate number you have.

options.text: The number of requests per day.
options.explanation: Cost is priced per token, not per request. Two requests can differ in size by a factor of 100.
